On the 200 BCE map, Iron Age chieftainships covers the far south of India: the hills and valleys of today's Kerala, Tamil Nadu and southern Karnataka, where local chiefs ruled alongside the first Tamil kings.

From about 1200 BCE people here used iron tools and weapons, farmed rice and millet, kept cattle and made black and red pottery. They buried their dead in stone circles, dolmens and large urns, which is why archaeologists speak of a megalithic culture. Sites such as Adichanallur and Kodumanal show iron working, gold, beads and trade.

The earliest Tamil poems, the Sangam literature, describe this world: hill chiefs called velir, cattle raids, bards who sang for gifts, and three crowned kings above them, the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas. Writing arrived in the form of Tamil Brahmi. By the 1st century BCE, Roman ships came for pepper; see Roman ships reach Muziris.
